questions.q: What are the four pieces this project builds to form a complete DAO governance system?
options: A governance token, a Governor contract, a timelock-controlled treasury, and a proposal UI
A wallet, an exchange, a bridge, and a faucet
A frontend, a database, a load balancer, and a CDN
A miner, a validator, a relayer, and an oracle
questions.explain: The lesson names these four pieces explicitly as the building blocks every real on-chain governance system is some variation of.

questions.q: What does the Governor contract in this architecture actually control?
options: The voting rules -- voting delay, voting period, quorum, and proposal threshold
The price of the governance token on exchanges
The gas price of every transaction on the network
The visual design of the frontend proposal UI
questions.explain: The Governor contract is described as the rules engine: it enforces voting delay, voting period, quorum, and who can submit a proposal.

questions.q: Why does the treasury sit behind a TimelockController instead of executing passed proposals immediately?
options: So a passed vote never moves money instantly -- there's a mandatory delay before execution
Because Solidity requires every contract to use a timelock
Because a timelock makes transactions free
Because it prevents the DAO from ever spending its own funds
questions.explain: The lesson states the timelock enforces a mandatory delay so a passed proposal's calls don't execute the instant voting ends.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which lesson builds the governance token and its delegation mechanics?
options: Lesson 14
Lesson 13
Lesson 16
Lesson 17
questions.explain: The roadmap table places the governance token and delegation work in Lesson 14, right after this kickoff.

questions.q: Why does this project verify the Governor and TimelockController syntax against OpenZeppelin's current documentation rather than relying on memory?
options: Because the governance API's exact shape has changed across OpenZeppelin's major versions
Because OpenZeppelin has never published documentation
Because Solidity itself has no stable syntax at all
Because memory-based code is always faster to compile
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes the Governance API has changed shape across versions, which is why each lesson verifies against current docs instead of guessing.
